s.def: A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form of communication.
ex: The English and German languages are both members of the West Germanic language family.
Deaf and mute people communicate using sign language.
He appears, and gives his advice, accompanied by a stone, which, by being put into the mouth, endows its possessor with the gift of all languages.

s.def: The ability to communicate using words.
ex: the gift of language

s.def: A sublanguage: the slang of a particular community or jargon of a particular specialist field.
ex: legal language; the language of chemistry

s.def: The expression of thought (the communication of meaning) in a specified way; that which communicates something, as language does.
ex: body language; the language of the eyes
A tale about themselves [is] told by people with help from the universal languages of their eyes, their hands, and even their shirting feet.
Birding had become like that for me. It is a language that, once learnt, I have been unable to unlearn.

s.def: A computer language; a machine language.
ex: In fact pointers are called references in these languages to distinguish them from pointers in languages like C and C++.

s.def: The particular words used in a speech or a passage of text.
ex: The language used in the law does not permit any other interpretation.
The language he used to talk to me was obscene.

s.def: The specific wording or style of a text, such as a law or a contract.
A body of sounds, signs or signals by which animals communicate, and by which plants are sometimes also thought to communicate.
ex: Prairie dogs use their language to refer to real dangers in the real world, so it definitely has meaning.

s.def: A manner of expression.
ex: Their language simple, as their manners meek, […]

s.def: Profanity.
ex: "Where the hell is Horace?" ¶ "There he is. He's coming. You shouldn't use language."

s.def: A short alphabetic or numeric identifier assigned to a language.
ex: af is the two-letter language code for Afrikaans.

s.def: A method of language learning based on mutual practice by learning partners who speak different languages.
A set of languages which have evolved from a common ancestor.
A school where foreign languages are taught

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-der. Latin langueō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin languidusder. Middle French languidebor. ▲ Latin languidusbor. English languid Borrowed from Middle French languide (“fatigued, weak; apathetic, indifferent”) (modern French languide), or from its etymon Latin languidus (“faint, weak; dull; slow, sluggish; ill, sick, unwell; (figuratively) inactive, inert, listless”), from langueō (“to be faint or weak; (figurative…

s.def: Of a person or animal, or their body functions: flagging from weakness, or inactive or weak, especially due to illness or tiredness; faint, listless.
Of a person or their movement: showing a dislike for physical effort; leisurely, unhurried.
ex: Loth was he to move / From the imprinted couch, and when he did, / 'Twas with slow, languid paces, and face hid / In muffling hands.
A consort was found for him in the royal family of France; and her beauty and grace gave him a languid pleasure.
Val watched his back, languid and slim, till it was out of sight …

s.def: Of a person or their actions, character, etc.: lacking drive, emotion, or enthusiasm; apathetic, listless, spiritless, unenthusiastic.
ex: I was languid and dull and very bad company when I wrote the above; I am better now, to my own feelings at least, and wish I may be more agreeable.
George had an air at once swaggering and melancholy, languid and fierce.

s.def: Of a colour: not bright; dull, muted.
Of an idea, writing, etc.: dull, uninteresting.
Of a period of time: characterized by lack of activity; pleasant and relaxed; unstressful.
Of a thing: lacking energy, liveliness, or strength; inactive, slow-moving, weak.
ex: languid breathing languid movements

s.def: Synonym of languet (“a flat plate in (or opposite and below the mouth of) the pipe of an organ”).

ety: From Middle English languysshen, from the present participle stem of Anglo-Norman and Middle French languir, from Late Latin languīre, alteration of Latin languēre (“to be faint, unwell”). : Compare languor, languid and lax. : Cognate with slack.

s.def: To lose strength and become weak; to be in a state of weakness or sickness.
ex: We […] do languish of such diseases.

s.def: To pine away in longing for something; to have low spirits, especially from lovesickness.
ex: He languished without his girlfriend.

s.def: To live in miserable or disheartening conditions.
ex: He languished in prison for years.

s.def: To be neglected; to make little progress, be unsuccessful.
ex: The case languished for years before coming to trial.

s.def: To make weak; to weaken, devastate.
To affect a languid air, especially disingenuously.
Lacking of vigor or spirit.
present participle and gerund of languish
The act of one who languishes.
ex: Happy, Monimia, he to whom these sighs, / These tears, and all these languishings, are paid!

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English langore, langour (“disease, illness; misery, sadness; suffering; condition or event causing sadness, suffering, etc.; unwholesomeness; idleness, inertia; depression, self-disgust; expression of grief”) [and other forms], from Middle French languer, langueur, langour, and Anglo-Norman langor, langour, langur, Old French langueur, languour (“disease, illness; suffering; emotional fatigue, sadness; listlessness; stagnation”) (modern French langueur (“languor…

s.def: A state of the body or mind caused by exhaustion or disease and characterized by a languid or weary feeling; lassitude; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: languor of convalescence

s.def: Melancholy caused by lovesickness, sadness, etc.; (countable) an instance of this.
Dullness, sluggishness; lack of vigour; stagnation.
ex: From languor she passed to the lightest vivacity; her temper became merry and wild in the extreme; she was all at once a tease, a tomboy, and a witch.

s.def: Listless indolence or inactivity, especially if enjoyable or relaxing; dreaminess; (countable) an instance of this.
Heavy humidity and stillness of the air.
ex: There is a languor in the air which encourages your own, and the poetry of memory is in every drooping flower and falling leaf.
[A] certain languor in the air hinted at an early summer.
The evening was mild, with a certain languor in the air.

s.def: Sorrow; suffering; also, enfeebling disease or illness; (countable, obsolete) an instance of this.
To languish.

ety: From Middle English lank, from Old English hlanc, from Proto-West Germanic *hlank, from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“lank, thin”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng- (“to bend, turn, wind, twist”); compare German lenken (“to turn”), Gelenk (“joint”), Old High German hlanca (“hip, side, flank”), and English link (of a chain).

s.def: Slender or thin; not well filled out; not plump; shrunken; lean.
ex: […] while I stood in the dark, a hand touched mine, lank fingers came feeling over my face, and I was sensible of a peculiar unpleasant odour.
Blacks in the fields, lank and stooped, their fingers spiderlike among the bolls of cotton.

s.def: Meagre, paltry, scant in quantity.
Straight and flat; thin and limp. (Often associated with being greasy.)
Languid; drooping, slack.
To become lank.
A clump of lank hair.

ety: From lank + -y.

s.def: Tall, slim, and rather ungraceful or awkward.
ex: tall and lanky
awkwardly lanky
long, lanky frame

ety: From Middle French lanier (“cowardly”), possibly from Latin lānārius.

s.def: The lanner falcon, Falco biarmicus.
ex: The mountains of this country also supply Saker falcons of excellent flight, and plenty of lanners likewise.

ety: From lanner + -et.

s.def: A male lanner, smaller than the female.

ety: Former trademark (1885-1902), from lāna (“wool”) + oleum (“oil”) + -in

s.def: A greasy yellow substance chemically akin to wax that is secreted from wooly animals, with a variety of uses from rust prevention, lubrication and waterproofing to cosmetics and skin ointments.
Alternative spelling of lanolin.
Alternative spelling of lanolin.

ety: Borrowed from French lansquenet, from German Landsknecht, from Lands (“of the land”) + Knecht (“servant”). Doublet of Landsknecht.

s.def: Any of a class of German mercenaries of the 15th and 16th centuries, most of whom were pikemen and foot soldiers.
ex: Ruthless killing, wanton strife / Add up to a lanzknecht’s life.

s.def: A gambling card game in which the dealer is given an initial card and the players another; cards are then turned up until the value (rank) of one of those cards is met.
ex: One could see part of the dimly lit court where under an enclosed poplar two soldiers on a stone bench were playing lansquenet.
And so it was over the game of lansquenet that I scored my first triumph.

ety: From Middle English lanterne (13th century), via Old French lanterne from Latin lanterna (“lantern”), itself a corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”) (see lamp, λάμπω (lámpō)) by influence of Latin lucerna (“lamp”). The spelling lanthorn was current during the 16th to 19th centuries and originates with a folk etymology associating the word with the use of horn as translucent cover. For the verb, compare French lanterner to hang at the lamppost. Displaced native Old English lēoht…

s.def: A case of translucent or transparent material made to protect a flame, or light, used to illuminate its surroundings.
Especially, a metal casing with lens used to illuminate a stage (e.g. spotlight, floodlight).
An open structure of light material set upon a roof, to give light and air to the interior.
A cage or open chamber of rich architecture, open below into the building or tower which it crowns.
A smaller and secondary cupola crowning a larger one, for ornament, or to admit light.
ex: the lantern of the cupola of the Capitol at Washington, or that of the Florence cathedral

s.def: A lantern pinion or trundle wheel.
A kind of cage inserted in a stuffing box and surrounding a piston rod, to separate the packing into two parts and form a chamber between for the reception of steam, etc.; a lantern brass.
A light formerly used as a signal by a railway guard or conductor at night.
A perforated barrel to form a core upon.
Aristotle's lantern

ety: From the carrying and displaying of lanterns during such festivals.

s.def: A festival marking the end of the Chinese New Year period, celebrated on the fifteenth day of the first month in the Chinese calendar when the first full moon of the year is seen (in February or early March).

ยี่เป็ง (Yi Peng), a festival celebrated chiefly in northern Thailand on the day of the full moon in the second month of the northern Thai lunar calendar (equivalent to the twelfth month of the lunar calendar used in the rest of Thailand, generally in November).

ety: From lanthanium + -ide.

s.def: A subset of the rare-earth elements
Any of the 15 rare earth elements from lanthanum to lutetium in the periodic table; because their outermost orbitals are not filled, they have very similar chemistry; below them are the actinides.
Any of the 14 rare earth elements from lanthanum to ytterbium (lutetium is excluded by some authors as it is a d-block rather than an f-block element).
Any of the 14 rare earth elements from cerium to lutetium (lanthanum having been excluded because it was thought to be a d-block element in the past).

ety: From Ancient Greek λανθάνω (lanthánō, “to escape notice”) + -um (“a chemical element”), because it had gone long undetected in mineral ores.

s.def: A chemical element (symbol La) with an atomic number of 57: a soft, ductile, silvery-white metal that tarnishes slowly when exposed to air.
An atom of this element.

ety: From late Middle English lainer, lainere, lanyer (“strap or thong used to fasten armour”) (with the ending modified in the 17th century under the influence of yard), from Old French laniere, lasniere (“thong, lash”) (see modern French lanière (“lanyard, strap”)). The French word is ultimately from Germanic, cognate with Old High German nestila (“band, headband; strap”) (modern German Nestel (“lace; strap; string”)), Old Norse nesta (“brace; fastener, strap”).

s.def: A short rope used for fastening rigging, as a handle, etc.
ex: "Take ahold here, an' keep ringin' steady," said Dan, passing Harvey the lanyard of a bell that hung just behind the windlass.

s.def: A cord worn around the neck, shoulder, or wrist which is attached to a small object to be carried such as an identity card or security pass, key, knife, or whistle.
A craft activity done by intricately braiding thin colored plastic lines to make patterns, or the product of such a craft.
ex: It's lanyard. It's a camp tradition. You'll have about a million lanyard key chains by the time the summer is over.
A few lousy days at Camp Minnehaha spent extracting oar splinters from your palms and taking group lanyard lessons under the full noonday sun.

A civil servant or mid-level bureaucrat, viewed as officious and overly concerned with social justice.
ex: Completely agree. Nowhere more so than in Scotlsnd^([sic]), where the lanyards are making a mockery of how a parliament should work.
DEI has allowed them to virtue signal and bolster their own positions simultaneously. Win-win for the lanyards.

ety: From Latin Lāodicēa, from Ancient Greek Λαοδίκεια (Laodíkeia), from Λαοδίκη (Laodíkē) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming place names”), chiefly after Laodice I and other Seleucid empresses. Equivalent to Laodice + -a.

Various former cities in West Asia, including
Galangal

ety: From Middle English lappe, from Old English læppa (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from Proto-West Germanic *lappō, from Proto-Germanic *lappô (“cloth; rag”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with Dutch lap (“cloth; rag”), German Lappen (“cloth; lobe; flap”), Icelandic leppur (“rag; patch”).

ety: From lap + board.

s.def: A board held on the lap as a simple lap desk.

ety: From lap + -el (“diminutive suffix”).

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English lapidari, lapidarie (“person who cuts, polishes, or engraves precious stones; expert in precious stones; treatise on precious stones”) [and other forms], from Old French lapidaire (“gemsmith, lapidary”) (modern French lapidaire), or from its etymon Latin lapidārius (“(adjective) of stones, stony; (noun) stonecutter”), from lapidis (the genitive singular of lapis (“stone; (poetic) jewel, precious stone”), possibly from Pre-Greek or Proto-Indo-European *lep…

An expert in gems and precious stones; a connoisseur of lapidary work.
Gems and precious stones collectively; jewellery.
A treatise on (precious) stones.

engraved on stone.

ex: the host (in tailcoat, grey cravat, purple vest) is lapidated by his wife while he loudly cries: "Maggie—please save a cup fer coffee in the morning."
On August 27, 2002, a Nigerian court ordered the mother of a newborn child, Amina Lawal, to be publicly lapidated for adultery.

s.def: To hurl insults at.
ex: The hour-long (and far too slow-paced) show: Malice in Wonderland, by lampooning, lapidating S. J. Perelman, veteran of movie-writing stints

ex: The five women on trial were almost all activists for the full repeal (not just a moratorium) of lapidation, ie stoning, from Iran’s law books.

Capable of being converted into stone.

Calcarius lapponicus, a passerine bird in the longspur family Calcariidae.

lapse of judgment

A fall or apostasy.

To fall into error or heresy.

ety: From lap (“upper legs of a seated person”) + top, modeled after desktop.

ex: He was playing a video game on his laptop.

ety: From Middle English lapwynge, lapwynke, lappewincke, lapwynche, lhapwynche, from Old English hlēapewince (“lapwing”), from Old English hlēapan (“to leap”) + wincian (“to wink, make a sign”), due to its manner of flight. Cognate with West Frisian ljip (“lapwing”). The modern form is influenced by folk etymology to resemble English wing.

ex: Lapwings are abundant winter visitors to the area but, like the Golden Plovers, vary greatly in number between years.

ex: This lapwing runs away with the shell on his head.

ety: From Middle English ladde-bord, latebord, most likely referring to the side of the ship on which cargo was loaded. Changed to larboard in the 1500s by association with starboard. s.def: The left side of a ship, looking from the stern forward to the bow; port side.
ex: The boat made a sharp half-turn to larboard, and then shot off in its new direction like a thunderbolt.
"It means to turn to larboard."

ety: Coined in Middle English (as larceni) between 1425 and 1475 from Anglo-Norman larcin (“theft”), from Latin latrocinium (“robbery”), from latro (“robber, mercenary”), from Ancient Greek λάτρον (látron, “pay, hire”). Doublet of latrociny.

s.def: The unlawful taking of personal property as an attempt to deprive the legal owner of it permanently.
ex: “Why are you walking around,” inquired Oedipa, “with your eyes closed, Metzger?” “Larceny,” Metzger said, “maybe they'll need a lawyer.”

s.def: An individual instance of such a taking.
ex: That young man already has four assaults, a DUI, and a larceny on his record.

ety: From early modern German Larche, Lärche, from Middle High German larche, from Old High German larihha, from Proto-West Germanic *larikā, an early borrowing from Latin larix, from Ancient Greek λάριξ (lárix), itself possibly of Gaulish origin.

s.def: A coniferous tree, of genus Larix, having deciduous leaves in fascicles.
Wood of the larch.

ety: From Middle English lard, from Old French lard (“bacon”), from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).

Excess fat on a person or animal.
To stuff (meat) with bacon or pork before cooking.
To smear with fat or lard.

ety: From the Latin plural lares, from lar, q.v.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Lares.

Along with big, it mostly displaced Middle English stoor and muchel (the latter surviving in much under a different meaning).

s.def: Of considerable or relatively great size or extent.
ex: Russia is a large country. The fruit-fly has large eyes for its body size. He has a large collection of stamps.
Test large, cylindrical, early portion closely coiled and always completely involute, later and larger portion uncoiled[…]
The largest age group for volunteers was 35-44, the CNCS survey said, and volunteers were most likely to be parents with children under 18.

Abundant; ample.

ex: I might be very large upon the importance and advantages of education.

s.def: Free; unencumbered.
ex: Of burdens all he set the Paynims large.

s.def: Unrestrained by decorum; said of language.
ex: Some large jests he will make.

An old musical note, equal to two longas, four breves, or eight semibreves.
Liberality, generosity.
A thousand dollars/pounds.

s.def: At some unspecified time in the future.
ex: I wanted to do it now, but I’ll have to do it later.

s.def: What if (something problematic or unanticipated happens); if not (something undesirable will happen).
ex: Compare Malay nanti (“later; if not”)
Later you fall asleep how?

der: shoot first and ask questions later

s.def: At some time in the future; subsequently; later.

ety: Borrowed from Latin laterālis (“belonging to the side”), from latus (“the side or flank”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

s.def: To the side; of or pertaining to the side.
ex: The medial side of the knee faces the other knee, while the outer side of the knee is lateral.
A fish senses changes in hydrodynamic pressure with its lateral line.

s.def: Non-linear or unconventional, as in, lateral thinking; outside the box.

(of a consonant, especially the English clear l) Pertaining to speech sounds generated by partially blocking the egress of the airstream with the tongue, leaving space on one or both sides of the occlusion for air passage.
An object, such as a passage or a protrusion, that is situated on the side of something else.
A sound produced through lateral pronunciation (such as /l/ in lateral).
A lateral pass.
An employee hired for a position at the same organizational level or salary as their previous position.
A lateral canal, a canal built alongside an existing stream.
ex: […] Canal and laterals, section 4, and the first part of section 5; and Miller Canal and laterals.

s.def: To move (oneself or something) in a lateral direction.
To execute a lateral pass.
Meristem forming a cylinder within some plants' organs (primarily stems, branches and roots) and allowing them to increase in girth (lateral growth).
name of a number of chronic, progressive nervous diseases.

ety: From Latin later (“brick”) + -ite.

s.def: A red hard or gravel-like soil or subsoil formed in the tropics that has been leached of soluble minerals leaving insoluble iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides; used to make bricks and roads.
ex: Constant tropical rain makes a mush of hard old lavas. The end product is a brick red soil called laterite.

ety: Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”). Potentially a borrowing from Ancient Greek λᾰ́τᾰξ (lắtăx, “drop of wine”), reformed by analogy to other nouns in -ex. The semantic shift, however, from drop of wine to water is difficult to explain and may indicate that both words originated from a separate language. Perhaps from the same root as Proto-Celtic *latis (Old Irish laith (“liquid, beer”), Wels…

s.def: The milky sap of several trees that coagulates on exposure to air; used to make rubber.
An emulsion of rubber in water, used in adhesives and the like.
A clear liquid believed to be a component of a humour or other bodily fluid (esp. plasma and lymph).
Natural latex rubber, especially nonvulcanized rubber, such as is used in making latex gloves, latex condoms, and latex clothing.

ety: From Middle English laththe, laþþe, earlier lathe, laþe, altered from Old English lætt (“lath”), from Proto-West Germanic *lattu, from Proto-Germanic *laþô (compare Dutch lat, German Latte) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lat- (compare Welsh llath (“rod, wand, yard”)).

s.def: A thin, narrow strip, fastened to the rafters, studs, or floor beams of a building, for the purpose of supporting a covering of tiles, plastering, etc.
ex: It is a piece of wood furnished with two parallel rows of plates, folding over each other, so as to resemble, in some degree, the laths of a blind.
"You are as thin as a lath and as brown as a nut."
Lanna says about wishing she was bigger in the chest and I goes that I had nothing to beat there and I was thin as a lat.

s.def: Microscopic, needle-like crystals, usually of plagioclase feldspar, in a glassy groundmass
One of the sharp-edged, thick planks driven forward to hold back loose earth or mud when digging the way through for tunnelling or spiling. Also called a spill.
To cover or line with laths.
Alternative form of lat (“staff; monumental pillar”).

ety: From Middle English lathen, from Old English laþian (“to invite, summon, call upon, ask”), from Proto-West Germanic *laþōn, from Proto-Germanic *laþōną (“to invite”), from Proto-Indo-European *lēy- (“to want, desire”). Cognate with German laden (“to invite”), Icelandic laða (“to attract”).

s.def: To invite; bid; ask.
An administrative division of the county of Kent, in England, from the Anglo-Saxon period until it fell entirely out of use in the early twentieth century.
A machine tool used to shape a piece of material, or workpiece, by rotating the workpiece against a cutting tool.
ex: He shaped the bedpost by turning it on a lathe.
The accidental amputation was due to the guard not being on the lathe.

s.def: The movable swing frame of a loom, carrying the reed for separating the warp threads and beating up the weft.
A granary; a barn.
To shape with a lathe.
To produce a three-dimensional model by rotating a set of points around a fixed axis.

ety: From Middle English lather, from Old English lēaþor (“a kind of nitre used for soap, soda”), from Proto-West Germanic *lauþr, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrą (“that which is used for washing, soap”), from Proto-Indo-European *lówh₃trom (“that which is used for washing”), from *lewh₃-, *lowh₃- (“to wash, bathe”). Cognate with Swedish lödder (“lather, foam, froth, soap”), Icelandic löður (“foam, froth, a kind of niter used for soap”), Old Irish loathar (“wash-basin”), Ancient Greek λουτρόν (loutrón,…

s.def: The foam made by rapidly stirring soap and water.
ex: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed.

s.def: Foam from profuse sweating, as of a horse.
A state of agitation.
To cover with lather.
ex: I lathered my body with lavender-scented soap.

s.def: To beat or whip.
To form lather or froth, as a horse does when profusely sweating.
ex: I woke Corporal Honda to see to the horse. Heavily lathered and breathing hard, it had obviously come a long way at high speed.

ety: Etymology tree English lather Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English lathery From lather + -y.

s.def: Resembling or covered in lather.
ex: This new shaving cream isn't as lathery as the old stuff: there just aren't as many bubbles to be had.
They wash their clothes in running streams with lathery weeds—too poor to buy soap.
He cleaned up the basin and flushed the lathery, hairy bits of toilet paper down the water closet.

ety: From Latin lātifundium, from lātus (“wide, extensive”) + fundus (“ground, base, estate, farm”). Doublet of latifundio.

s.def: A great landed estate with absentee ownership and labor often in a state of partial servitude.
ex: His vision for the future of the African continent in the Age of the Aerotropolis seems to be as a vast latifundium sown with GM wheat.

ety: From Middle English Latyn, Latyne, Latin, from Old French latin, latyn, from Latin latīnus, from Latium (“the region around Rome”) + -īnus (adjective suffix). Displaced or merged with Old English Lǣden. Doublet of Ladin and Ladino.

s.def: Of or relating to the script of the language spoken in ancient Rome and many modern alphabets.
ex: The Serbo-Croatian incunabula printed in Latin letters are indubitably the products of a very modest establishment.

s.def: Of or from Latin America or of Latin American culture.
ex: As such, today's Latin music is a synthesis of European, African, and the few indigenous elements that remain.

s.def: The language of the ancient Romans, other Latins and of the Roman Catholic church, especially Classical Latin.
ex: When the Christian Church rose in stature in the Dark Ages, its adoption of Latin as the official language assured its eternal life.
Like Copernicus and Galileo, Johannes Kepler was a renowned astronomer who wrote in Latin.

s.def: A person native to ancient Rome or its Empire.
ex: This appears incontestably from the manner in which the Latins wrote Greek words and names[…]

s.def: Of or relating to Latin: the language spoken in ancient Rome and other cities of Latium.
Of or relating to ancient Rome or its Empire.
ex: The earliest Latin culture of Ireland was heavily indebted to that of Britain[…]

s.def: Of or relating to Latium (modern Lazio), the region around Rome.
Of or relating to the customs and people descended from the ancient Romans and their Empire.
Roman Catholic; of or pertaining to the Roman Rite of the Catholic Church.
ex: The Latin bishop now took the Greek bishop by the hand and conducted him to his throne[…]

s.def: The Latin alphabet or writing system.

ety: Latin + alphabet.

s.def: The 26-letter alphabet consisting of the following letters (presented in majuscule and minuscule pairs)
ex: A a, B b, C c, D d, E e, F f, G g, H h, I i, J j, K k, L l, M m, N n, O o, P p, Q q, R r, S s, T t, U u, V v, W w, X x, Y y, Z z

s.def: Any relatively minor variation of the 26-letter Latin alphabet.

ety: Calque of French Amérique latine. Thought to be coined by French Emperor Napoleon III.

s.def: parts of the Americas which speak Spanish or Portuguese
Those parts of the Americas which speak Romance (Latin-derived) languages, namely Spanish, Portuguese, French, or creoles based on these.

A continental region consisting of those parts of the Americas located south of the United States where Spanish or Portuguese is predominantly spoken; sometimes including areas speaking French or French-based creoles.
Ibero-America (excluding all French-speaking areas).
umbrella term for South America, Central America, Mexico and the Caribbean (including English and Dutch-speaking areas).
One of the 24 particular churches (sui juris) in full communion with the Holy See and the rest of the Catholic Church which uses the Latin liturgical rites.
Western Christianity.

ety: From Latinize + -ation.

s.def: The act or process of Latinizing, of making Latin; including translating into Latin.

ety: The gender-neutral suffix -x replaces the gendered suffixes -a and -o. Reinforced by United States Spanish latinx.

s.def: A Latin person (of any gender); a Latino or Latina.
ex: (which see for more)
@nmoon Looks can be deceiving, but I "see" no Latinx, several multi-racials, 3 whites 90% AfrAm. I don't see anyone who looks solely AsAmer
@metalmujer @soylamar there's also a variant with an x (Latinxs, maestrxs, etc.) but not quite as popular as @

ety: Etymology tree English late Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -isch English -ish English latish From late + -ish.

s.def: Somewhat late
Somewhat late
ex: We'll be home latish, perhaps not until 10 p.m.

ety: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus. Possibly related with lateral, though this is uncertain.

s.def: The angular distance north or south from a planet's equator, measured along the meridian of that particular point.
ex: The oat is hardier than wheat, and ripens in higher latitudes.

s.def: The relative freedom from restrictions; scope to do something.
ex: His parents gave him a great deal of latitude.

s.def: An imaginary line (in the form of a circumference) around a planet running parallel to the planet's equator.
ex: snow showers in the northerly latitudes

s.def: The angular distance of a heavenly body from the ecliptic.
The extent to which a light-sensitive material can be over- or underexposed and still achieve an acceptable result.
Extent or scope; e.g. breadth, width or amplitude.

ety: From Latin lātitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin lātitūdō, from lātus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, latitude + -arian.

s.def: Not restrained; not confined by precise limits.
Tolerant, especially of other people's religious views.
Lax in moral or religious principles.
A person who is tolerant of others' religious views.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Latium. Doublet of Lazio.

s.def: A historical region of central Italy, in which the city of Rome was founded and grew to be the capital city of the Roman Empire.
Lazio: A modern administrative region of central Italy.

ety: From French latrine (“latrine”), from Latin lātrīna.

s.def: Any facility or device used for urination or defecation, whether toilet, lavatory, or outhouse.
A chamber pot.
An open trench or pit used for urination and defecation.

ety: Ellipsis of caffè latte, from Italian caffellatte, ultimately from Latin lac, lactis.

s.def: Affluent leftism.
ex: latte liberal

s.def: A drink of coffee made from espresso and steamed milk, generally topped with foam.
ex: Lilian Benedict walked into the office carrying two cups of latte.
High-priced lattes and customized drinks helped lift the coffee chain’s US sales in the quarter ending on October 1, the company said Thursday.

s.def: A similar drink, where the espresso is replaced with some other flavoring ingredient such as chai, maté or matcha (green tea).
ex: matcha latte

ety: From Middle English laten, latun, latoun, from Old French laton, laiton, from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, “copper, copper alloy”), itself from Proto-Common Turkic *altun (“gold”). See Turkish altın, Old Turkic 𐰞𐱃𐰆𐰣 (altun, “gold”), Karakhanid اَلْتُونْ (altūn, “gold”).

s.def: An alloy of copper and tin, similar to bronze, with a sufficient portion of tin to make it a pewter-like color with yellowish tinge (rather than the brownish-gold color of bronze of higher copper content), once used in thin sheets and for domestic utensils and light-duty tools.
Sheet tin; iron plate, covered with tin.
Any metal in thin sheets.

ety: From Middle English latter, lattere, lattre, from Old English lætra, comparative form of læt (“late”). Equivalent to late + -er, thus a doublet of later; also, related to last, whose doublet is latest.

s.def: Near (or nearer) to the end.
ex: the latter part of the century

s.def: In the past, but close (or closer) to the present time.
ex: In his latter years my dad became very absent-minded.

s.def: The second of aforementioned two items.
ex: The archaic past participle shapen is only used in misshapen, ill-shapen, and well-shapen (the latter two are much less common, though).
the difference between reason and revelation, and in what sense the latter is superior

ety: From Middle English latis, from Middle French lattis (“lathing”), from Old French lattis, from latte (“a lath”), from Frankish *lattu (“a lath”), from Proto-Germanic *laþô (“board; plank; ledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)latn-, *(s)lat- (“beam; log”). Cognate with Old High German latta (“lath”), (German Latte), Old English lætt (“lath”), Middle Low German lāde (“plank, counter, sales counter”), German Laden (“shop”). More at lath.

s.def: A flat panel constructed with widely-spaced crossed thin strips of wood or other material, commonly used as a garden trellis.
A bearing with vertical and horizontal bands that cross each other.
A regular spacing or arrangement of geometric points, often decorated with a motif.
A model of the tuning relationships of a just intonation system, comprising an array of points in a periodic multidimensional pattern.

In any of several technical senses, a substructure with properties analogous to those the set of points with integer coordinates bears in relation to the full Euclidian space these points are contained in.
A partially ordered set in which every pair of elements has a unique supremum and a unique infimum.
To make a lattice of.
ex: to lattice timbers

s.def: To close, as an opening, with latticework; to furnish with a lattice.
ex: to lattice a window

ety: Borrowed from Latvian Latvija.

s.def: A country in northeastern Europe. Official name: Republic of Latvia. Capital: Riga.

ety: Etymology tree Latvian Latvijabor. English Latvia Middle English -n English -n English Latvian From Latvia + -n.

s.def: Of, from, or pertaining to Latvia, the Latvian people or the Latvian language.
The official language of Latvia; Lettish.
A person from Latvia or of Latvian descent.
Latvian Soviet Socialist Republic, the name of Latvia when it was a member republic of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (1940–1941 and 1944–1991).

ety: Inherited from Middle English lauden, from Old French lauder, from Latin laudō, laudāre, from laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”), from echoic Proto-Indo-European root *leh₁wdʰ- (“song, sound”). Cognate with Old English lēoþ (“song, poem”), German Lied (“song”). Doublet of leed.

s.def: Glorification or praise.
ex: Laud be to God

s.def: Hymn of praise.
A prayer service following matins.
To praise; to glorify.

ety: From Middle English laudable, from Old French laudable or directly from Latin laudabilis; equivalent to laud + -able.

s.def: Worthy of being lauded.
ex: Near-synonym: admirable
laudable motives
laudable actions

s.def: Healthful; having a disposition to promote healing.
ex: laudable juices of the body
laudable pus

ety: From New Latin, from lādanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λᾱ́δανον (lā́danon). Originally the same word as ladanum, labdanum, compare French laudanum, Italian laudano, ladano. Perhaps influenced by Latin laudō (“to praise”). See ladanum. Used by Paracelsus to refer to ladanum gum, and to a compound recipe containing pearls, but apparently not to any preparation of opium; this modern sense was introduced by his followers (Sigerist 1941:540–1).

s.def: Any of several tinctures of opium, once widely used for various medical purposes and as a recreational drug.
ex: Whatever else was wanting to a wise man's happiness, —of laudanum I would have given him as much as he wished, and in a golden cup.
Whipping and abuse are like laudanum; you have to double the dose as the sensibilities decline.
Laudanum, a derivative of opium, was the name given to a secret remedy concocted by the occultist Paracelsus, in the sixteenth century.

s.def: To add laudanum to (a drink or the like).
To cause (a person) to be high on laudanum.

ety: Borrowed from Latin laudatio; compare Old English taudation. See laud.

s.def: The act of lauding; high praise or commendation.
ex: […] his wondrous laudations and defendings of the unfriended Turner […]

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *klek- Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan Old English hliehhander. Old English hlæhhan Middle English laughen, laghen English laugh From Middle English laughen, laghen, from (Anglian) Old English hlæhhan, hlehhan, (West Saxon) hliehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną. Cognates Germanic: Scots lauch (“to laugh”), Yola leeigh, leigh (“to laugh”), North Frisian laache, lachi, laake, loache, lååke (“to laugh”)…

s.def: An expression of mirth particular to the human species; the sound heard in laughing; laughter.
ex: And the loud laugh that spoke the vacant mind.
That man is a bad man who has not within him the power of a hearty laugh.
It never fails to get a laugh. Here's to more humor in chess.

s.def: Something that provokes mirth or scorn.
ex: Life's a piece of shit / When you look at it / Life's a laugh and death's a joke, it's true.
Your new hat's an absolute laugh, dude.

s.def: A fun person.
ex: a good laugh

s.def: To show mirth, satisfaction, or derision, by peculiar movement of the muscles of the face, particularly of the mouth, causing a lighting up of the face and eyes, and usually accompanied by the emission of explosive or chuckling sounds from the chest and throat; to indulge in laughter.
ex: There were many laughing children running on the school grounds.
The waves beside them danced, but they / Outdid the sparkling waves in glee:— / A Poet could not but be gay / In such a laughing company: […]
If life seems jolly rotten / There's something you've forgotten / And that's to laugh and smile and dance and sing.

s.def: To be or appear cheerful, pleasant, mirthful, lively, or brilliant; to sparkle; to sport.
To make an object of laughter or ridicule; to make fun of; to deride; to mock.
ex: Don't laugh at my new hat, man!
On the corner is a banker with a motorcar / The little children laugh at him behind his back

s.def: To affect or influence by means of laughter or ridicule.
To express by, or utter with, laughter.
ex: Fairfax addressed her as "my lady," she laughed her musical laugh, and glanced up at a picture of Gerald with eyes full of exultation.
"You refuse to take me seriously," Lute said, when she had laughed her appreciation. "How can I take that Planchette rigmarole seriously?"

s.def: to laugh in secret or to oneself, usually gloatingly
To laugh uproariously.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *klek- Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan Old English hliehhander. Old English hlæhhan Middle English laughen, laghen English laugh Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English laughable From laugh + -able.

s.def: Fitted to excite laughter; humorous.
ex: At this our first dinner at the Government House a very laughable incident occurred.

s.def: Worthless; worthy of contempt or derision.

ety: From Middle English laughynge; equivalent to laugh + -ing.

s.def: verbal noun of laugh: the action of the verb to laugh.
present participle and gerund of laugh
verbal adjective of laugh: the action of the verb to laugh.
A small pigeon (Spilopelia senegalensis) native to the tropics in Africa south of the Sahara; the Middle East; and southern Asia east to India.

ety: From its euphoric effects. Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1799.

s.def: Nitrous oxide, especially when used as an anaesthetic.

ety: From laughing + stock (“source, supply; butt, target”). Compare also whipping-stock, jesting-stock.

s.def: An object of ridicule, someone who is publicly ridiculed; the butt of a joke.
ex: Pray you let us not be laughing-stocks to other men's humours.
When he talked, he talked nonsense, and made himself the laughing-stock of his hearers.
If anyone can restore dignity to a franchise that has been close to a laughing stock in the last few years, it's Gibbs.

ety: From Middle English laughter, laghter, laȝter, from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”). Cognate with German Gelächter (“laughter, hilarity, merriment”), Danish and Norwegian latter (“laughter”), Icelandic hlátur (“laughter”). More at laugh.

s.def: The sound of laughing, produced by air so expelled; any similar sound.
ex: Their loud laughter betrayed their presence.
There was some laughter, and Roddle was left free to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town.

s.def: A movement (usually involuntary) of the muscles of the laughing face, particularly of the lips, and of the whole body, with a peculiar expression of the eyes, indicating merriment, satisfaction or derision, and usually attended by a sonorous and interrupted expulsion of air from the lungs.
ex: Archly the maiden smiled, and with eyes overrunning with laughter.

s.def: A reason for merriment.

ety: From Middle English launchen (“to throw as a lance”), Old French lanchier, another form (Old Northern French/Norman variant, compare Jèrriais lanchi) of lancier, French lancer, from lance.

s.def: To start (a program or feature); to execute or bring into operation.
ex: Double-click an icon to launch the associated application.
If the game does not automatically launch, select Disney Cory in the House from the DS launch screen.

s.def: To start to operate.
ex: After clicking the icon, the application will launch.

s.def: To throw (a projectile such as a lance, dart or ball); to hurl; to propel with force.
ex: There they were met by four thousand Ha'apa'a warriors, who launched a volley of stones and spears[…]

s.def: To pierce with, or as with, a lance.
ex: And launch your hearts with lamentable wounds.

s.def: To cause (a vessel) to move or slide from the land or a larger vessel into the water; to set afloat.
ex: The navy launched another ship.

s.def: To cause (a rocket, balloon, etc., or the payload thereof) to begin its flight upward from the ground.
ex: NASA launched several unmanned rockets before launching any of the Mercury astronauts.

s.def: To send out; to start (someone) on a mission or project; to give a start to (something); to put in operation
ex: Our business launched a new project.
Here was my chance. I took the old man aside, and two or three glasses of Old Crow launched him into reminiscence.
In mid-December 1944, the Germans launched a massive assault in what became known as the Battle of the Bulge.

s.def: To release; to put onto the market for sale
ex: On September 3rd Bionym, a Canadian firm, launched Nymi, a bracelet which detects the wearer’s heartbeat.

s.def: Of a ship, rocket, balloon, etc.: to depart on a voyage; to take off.
To move with force and swiftness like a sliding from the stocks into the water; to plunge; to begin.
ex: to launch into an argument or discussion
to launch into lavish expenditures

s.def: The surface or structure from which a launch is made.
A starting point.

ety: From launch + -er.

s.def: One who or that which launches. A device that throws something or the person who initiates a launch.
ex: The catapult made a good launcher for the small projectile.
They shot down the helicopter with a rocket launcher.

s.def: An application that launches another or others, often holding icons or menus for frequently used programs.
present participle and gerund of launch
The act by which something is launched; a launch.
ex: The launching of the Titanic.
By 1940 they had conducted 25 successful launchings of A5 rockets, which reached 10 miles altitude and had a range of 12 miles.

ety: Contracted from Middle English lavender, from Old French lavandiere, from Late Latin lavandera, from Latin lavō (“to wash”).

s.def: A washerwoman or washerman.
A trough used by miners to receive powdered ore from the box where it is beaten, or for carrying water to the stamps, or other apparatus for comminuting (sorting) the ore.
A trough or channel carrying water to the wheel of a watermill.
A gutter (for rainwater).
To wash; to wash, and to smooth with a flatiron or mangle; to wash and iron.
To lave; to wet.
ex: Oft did she heave her napkin to her eyne, / Which on it had conceited characters, / Laundering the silken figures in the brine

s.def: To disguise the source of (ill-gotten wealth) by various means.
To obtain a pointer to an object created in storage occupied by an existing object of the same type, even if it has const or reference members.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-der. Proto-Italic *lowō Latin lavo Latin lavareder. Latin lavandarium Latin lavandaria Old French lavanderiebor. Middle English lavendrie English laundry Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew Proto-Indo-European *tó- Proto-Hellenic *autós Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewder. Ancient Greek αὖ (aû) Ancient Greek τόν (tón) Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós) Ancient Greek αὐτο- (auto-) Proto-Indo-European *men- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *mn̥tós Proto-Hellenic *mə…

s.def: A self-service laundry facility with (traditionally) coin-operated (which now may use other per-load payment methods) washing machines, dryers, and sometimes ironing or pressing machines, open to the public for washing clothing and household cloth items.
A money laundering operation.

ety: From Middle English lavendrie, from Old French lavanderie, from Latin lavandaria. See launder.

s.def: A laundering; a washing.
ex: In our family of five, we have to do the laundry every other day.

s.def: A place or room where laundering is done - including, by extension, other forms of laundering than clothes washing.
That which needs to be, is being, or has been laundered.
ex: You've left your dirty laundry all over the house.

s.def: A penalty flag.
A business whose primary purpose is to conceal the origins of money received illegally.

der: air one's dirty laundry in public

ety: laundry + basket

s.def: A container, often made of plastic, for holding and transporting clothing and household textiles, especially before and after being laundered.

ety: From French loxodromique, from Ancient Greek λοξός (loxós, “oblique”) + δρόμος (drómos, “course”).

ety: Borrowed from Middle French loyal, from Old French loial, leial, leal, from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of legal and leal.

ety: From Middle English losenge, from Old French losenge (“rhombus”), of uncertain origin.

To mark or emblazon with a lozenge.

ety: From Middle English, perhaps from Old French lobeor (“swindler”), from Old French lober to mock, to jeer, or of Scandinavian origin, compare dialectal Swedish lubber. The grasshopper was likely so called after sense 1 (“a clumsy or lazy person”).

Alteration of rubber.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus (“slippery”). Doublet of lubricious.

ety: From French lucidité, from Late Latin lūciditās. By surface analysis, lucid + -ity.

ety: From Middle English Lucifer, from Latin Lūcifer (from lūx (“light”) + ferō (“bear, carry”)). Attested in Old English as Lūċifer. s.def: The King of Babylon who was compared to the planet Venus in first the Wycliffe version then the King James Version of Isaiah 14:12; it is unclear whether this verse refers to a specific king or to a representation of the entire line of kings of Babylon.
The planet Venus as the daystar (the morning star).
ex: Near-synonyms: Vesper, Hesperus, evening star, Venus

s.def: Satan, the Devil.

ety: From Middle English luk, lukke, from Middle Dutch luc, geluc, gelucke (“good luck, fortune”) or Middle Low German lücke, gelücke (“lot, fortune, fate, luck”), of obscure origin; perhaps ultimately related to German Lücke (“gap, opening”) in the sense of "space or opportunity", hence "chance". s.def: Something that happens to someone by chance, a chance occurrence.
ex: The raffle is just a matter of luck.
Gilbert had some bad luck yesterday — he got pick-pocketed and lost fifty dollars.

s.def: A superstitious feeling that brings fortune or success.
ex: He blew on the dice for luck.

Shepard: We better get moving. Dr. Warren: Good luck, Commander. Dr. Manuel: Luck won't save you.

s.def: Success.
ex: I tried for ages to find a pair of blue suede shoes, but didn't have any luck.

ety: From Middle English lukky, equivalent to luck + -y. Cognate with Scots lucky (“lucky”), West Frisian lokkich (“lucky, fortunate”), Dutch gelukkig (“lucky, fortunate, happy”). a lucky cast

ety: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin lūcubrātus, perfect passive participle of lūcubrō (“to work by candlelight”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lūx (“light”).

ety: From French ludique, from Latin ludo (“to play”).

ex: The lugworms were shorter and lighter, with hispid gills and mucus-coloured tails.

ety: From Middle English lullen, lollen. Originally, perhaps expressive in origin from la-la-la or lu-lu-lu sounds made in calming a child. ex: The storm lulled.

ety: From Middle English lullen (“to lull”) + bye. First recorded c. 1560. Compare Old English bī, bī (“lullaby!”, interjection).

ety: The noun is borrowed from Late Latin lumbāgō (“backache of the lumbar region”), from Late Latin lumbus (“lumbar”), Latin lumbus (“loin”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loins”)) + -āgō (suffix forming nouns describing objects, animals, and plants). ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *lewk- Proto-Indo-European *-s- Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *léwksmn̥ Proto-Italic *louksmən Latin lumen Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-sḱéti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁sḱeti Proto-Italic *-ēskō Latin -ēscō Latin -escensder. English -escence English luminescence From Latin lumen + English -escence.

s.def: Any emission of light that cannot be attributed merely to the temperature of the emitting body.

ety: From Latin lumen, lumin- (“light”, noun) + -ferous [from ferre (“to bear, carry”, verb) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives)].

s.def: Producing or transmitting light; luminous.

ety: First use appears in 1934 in a paper by E. Huntress, L. Stanley, and A. Parker. The verbal form first appears c. 1997, although the exact date of its first appearance is uncertain.

s.def: The compound 5-amino-2,3-dihydro-1,4-phthalazinedione, which exhibits blue chemiluminescence when mixed with an appropriate oxidizing agent.

ety: Borrowed from French luminosité or else a native formation from luminous + -ity.

s.def: the state of being luminous, or a luminous object; brilliance or radiance
ex: They reported encountering a luminosity of great intensity and loving angelic beings.

s.def: The rate at which a star radiates energy in all directions.
ex: We recognize the same pattern as in the left panel, with dM stars being much less frequent flarers than dMe stars of similar luminosity.

s.def: the ratio of luminous flux to radiant flux at the same wavelength; the luminosity factor

ety: Borrowed from Middle French lumineus, from Latin lūminōsus.

s.def: Emitting light; glowing brightly; shining.
ex: The bonfire in his heart made luminous the rose-tan in his cheek.

s.def: Brightly illuminated.
Clear; enlightening; easy to understand.
ex: a luminous explanation

ety: Unknown. First attested in 1825 in East Anglian slang. Perhaps from "dumb ox", influenced by lumbering; or from or cognate to dialectal verb lummock (“move about heavily or clumsily”), itself a word of uncertain origin.

s.def: A clumsy, stupid person; an awkward bungler.
ex: You've broken the plates, you great lummox!
I love you, Gal. You're lovable. Big lovable bloke. Loveable lump. Loveable lummox. Gal Dove, party boy. Big oaf.

ety: From Middle English lumpe, from a Germanic base akin to Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, go, hang loosely”). Compare Dutch lomp (“rag”), German Low German Lump (“rag”), German Lumpen (“rag”) and Lump (“ragamuffin”).

s.def: Something that protrudes, sticks out, or sticks together; a cluster or blob; a mound or mass of no particular shape.
ex: Stir the gravy until there are no more lumps.
a lump of coal; a lump of clay; a lump of cheese

s.def: A swelling or nodule of tissue under the skin or in an internal part of the body.
ex: Lumps in the breasts are an indicator of breast cancer.

s.def: A group, set, or unit.
ex: The money arrived all at once as one big lump sum payment.

s.def: A small, shaped mass of sugar, typically about a teaspoonful.
ex: Do you want one lump or two with your coffee?

s.def: A dull or lazy person.
ex: Don't just sit there like a lump.

s.def: A fat person.
A beating or verbal abuse.
ex: He's taken his lumps over the years.
Komer admitted that the United States would probably suffer "short term lumps" as a result of Johnson's brusque decision.

s.def: A projection beneath the breech end of a gun barrel.
A kind of fish, the lumpsucker.
ex: You roast him [the fish] […] just like a lump.

s.def: Food given to a tramp to be eaten on the road.

der: bring a lump to someone's throat

s.def: A small sledgehammer, intended for single-handed use.

ety: From lun(atic) + -acy.

s.def: The state of being mad, insanity
Something deeply misguided.

ety: From Middle English lunar (“shaped like the crescent moon”), from Latin lūnāris (“of or pertaining to the moon, lunar”) (possibly through Middle French lunaire (modern French lunaire (“lunar”)), from lūna (“the Moon; crescent shape”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”)) + -is (suffix forming adjectives).

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the Moon (that is, Luna, the Earth's moon).
ex: lunar observations a lunar eclipse

s.def: Shaped like a crescent moon; lunate.
Extremely high.
ex: Julian wolfed down the rest of his dinner and when he accompanied Michelle back to her apartment his spirits were positively lunar.
House prices were in freefall, if you owned one. They remained laughably lunar to the rent-bound.

s.def: (Believed to be) influenced by the Moon, as in character, growth, or properties.
Of or pertaining to silver (which was symbolically associated with the Moon by alchemists).
Of or pertaining to travel through space between the Earth and the Moon, or exploration and scientific investigation of the Moon.
The middle bone of the proximal series of the carpus in the wrist, which is shaped like a half-moon.
ex: There are two larger bones of the wrist called the scaphoid and lunar; these form a large ball, and this is received into the lower end of the radius.
The scaphoid and lunar (wrist bones) are separate, whereas in Carnivores they are united perhaps to give greater strength to the wrist.

s.def: An observation of a lunar distance (“the angle between the Moon and another celestial body”), especially for establishing the longitude of a ship at sea.
A calendar that measures the passage of the year according to the phases of the moon, as opposed to the revolution of the earth around the sun; a calendar of the lunar year.
A phenomenon occurring when the Earth casts a shadow over the Moon.
The spacecraft used in the Apollo missions that was designed for the landing on the surface of the Moon; the lunar excursion module.
Alternative letter-case form of Lunarian.

ety: First attested in 1777; borrowed from Latin lūnātus (“crescent-shaped”), from lūna (“moon”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Shaped like a crescent.
ex: a lunate beak

s.def: A small stone artifact, probably an arrowhead, with a blunt straight edge and a sharpened, crescent-shaped back, especially characteristic of the Mesolithic Period.
The lunate bone.

ety: From Middle English lunatik, from Old French lunatique, from Late Latin lunaticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin luna (“moon”), the connection stemming from the belief that changes of the moon caused intermittent insanity.

s.def: An insane person.
ex: You may be right I may be crazy Oh, but it just may be a lunatic you're looking for

s.def: Crazed, mad, insane, demented.
Relating to the Moon; lunar.
Influenced or affected by the Moon.
ex: This I remember: she was false as the lunatic sea.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lūnātiō.

s.def: A month of an average of approximately 29.53 days, measured from a lunar phase until the return of that same phase.
ex: And there is not the moon seen in all the lunation, save only the second quarter.

s.def: The irregular period from one new moon until the next.

ety: Recorded since 1580 in the sense “piece, hunk”. The word luncheon with the same meaning is presumably an extension on the pattern of puncheon (“cask”) and truncheon (“cudgel”). But earliest found forms of luncheon include lunshin and lunching, which are equivalent to lunch + -ing, with the suffix -ing possibly later modified to imitate a French origin. In contrast, the more common sense “light meal” is first attested for luncheon in 1652 and for lunch in 1829, so in this sense the latter is pro…

s.def: A light meal usually eaten around midday, notably when not as main meal of the day.
ex: We made an odd party before the arrival of the Ten, particularly when the Celebrity dropped in for lunch or dinner.

s.def: A break in play between the first and second sessions.
Any small meal, especially one eaten at a social gathering.
ex: After the funeral there was a lunch for those who didn't go to the cemetery.

s.def: A thin piece or hunk (of bread, meat, etc.)
To eat lunch.
ex: I like to lunch in Italian restaurants.
The gentleman had left for London after lunch. Yes, alone; but he had lunched in the hotel with a lady.
Miss Otis regrets she's unable to lunch today.

s.def: To treat to lunch.
ex: We dined him, we lunched him, we were photographed in his company by flashlight.

ety: From lunch + break.

s.def: A period of rest from work for the purpose of eating lunch.

ety: Of uncertain origin. Possibly derived from an earlier *lumpchin, *lumpchen, a diminutive of lump (“chunk, parcel of food, lunch”), thus related to lunch. It is unclear which came first: whether lunch is a shortening of luncheon, or whether luncheon is an augmentation of lunch. Possibly also a dissimilatory form of or influenced by nuncheon (“light snack taken in the afternoon”). Noun sense 2 (“sausage”) is likely a ellipsis of luncheon sausage or luncheon meat.

s.def: A formal meal served in the middle of the day.
ex: Most people thought the food at the luncheon was mediocre.

s.def: A large, cheap, processed sausage served in thin slices.
ex: Ian bought the luncheon since it was on special.
Filled Roll (x2) 1x luncheon, tomato, lettuce, and mayonnaise / 1x cheese and onion

s.def: Any midday meal; lunch.
ex: "Have you had luncheon?"

s.def: A lump of food.
A portion of food taken at any time except at a regular meal; an informal or light repast.
To eat luncheon.
To serve luncheon to.
ex: A number of friends of Mrs. H. M. Richey, wife of H. M., luncheoned her on Thursday at the Warden Hotel.
To soften him up, a group of his fellows luncheoned him at the Jonathan Club in Los Angeles.
There must have been a chip of the blarney stone in the Irish stew the pretty stewardess luncheoned us with, for one quipped.

ety: Etymology tree English lunch Proto-Indo-European *Hrew-? Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH-der. Proto-Germanic *rūmą Proto-West Germanic *rūm Old English rūm Middle English roum English room English lunchroom From lunch + room.

s.def: A room designated as a place to eat lunch.
ex: Company policy was to eat snacks only in the lunchroom.

s.def: A diner or small restaurant that serves lunch.
ex: I don't know how they stay in business serving only lunch, but the lunchroom on the corner is cheap and fast so I like it.

ety: From lunch + time.

s.def: The time or hour at or around which lunch is normally eaten.
A break in work or school to eat lunch.
ex: It's almost lunchtime, so I think I'll finish up later this afternoon.

ety: From Latin lūna (“moon”).

s.def: A fit of lunacy or madness; a period of frenzy; a crazy or unreasonable freak.
ex: Why woman, your husband is in his olde Lunes againe: […]

s.def: A concave figure formed by the intersection of the arcs of two circles on a plane, or on a sphere the intersection between two great semicircles.
Anything crescent-shaped.
A leash for a hawk.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French lunette, diminutive of lune (“moon”).

s.def: A small opening in a vaulted roof of a circular or crescent shape.
ex: Next came the semi-landing with the lunette window, and here the door opened under the pressure of a single finger, and with a sigh and creak.

s.def: A crescent-shaped recess or void in the space above a window or door.
An image or other representation of a crescent moon.
A field work consisting of two projecting faces forming a wedge each of which extends from one of two parallel flanks.
ex: This Lunette, as we have seen, was confronted, and even in siege-form "approached", by a part of Canrobert's army [...].

s.def: A luna: a crescent-shaped receptacle, often glass, for holding the (consecrated) host (the bread of communion) upright when exposed in the monstrance.
A type of flattened glass used in watch-making.
ex: Lunette and double lunette glasses are generally sized in quarters; crystals and thin flat lunettes for hunters in eighths.

s.def: The circular hole in the guillotine in which the victim's neck is placed.
A type of crescent-shaped dune blown up along a lake basin, especially in dry areas of Australia.
ex: Sticking out of a crescent-shaped sand ridge of a type known as a lunette were some human bones.

s.def: A half horseshoe, lacking the sponge.
A piece of felt to cover the eye of a vicious horse.

ety: From Middle English lunge, longe, from Old English lungen, from Proto-Germanic *lunganjō, an enlargement of *lungô (“the light organ, lung”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-, whence ultimately also light. Cognate with West Frisian long, Dutch long, German Lunge, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk lunge, Swedish lunga, Icelandic lunga, and also Russian лёгкое (ljóxkoje) (lung), Ancient Greek ἐλαφρός (elaphrós, “light in weight”) and perhaps Albanian lungë (“blister, bulge”). Com…

s.def: That which supplies oxygen or fresh air, such as trees, parklands, forest, etc., to a place.
A biological organ of vertebrates that controls breathing and oxygenates the blood.
Capacity for exercise or exertion; breath.
ex: He no longer has the lungs to play long rallies like he used to.

s.def: Carcinoma of the lungs, cancer that begins in the lung(s), but can metastasize to virtually any tissue.
Any tumor, especially a malignant one, occurring in the lungs.

ety: From French allonge, from Old French alonge, from alongier, from Vulgar Latin *allongare, from ad + Late Latin longare, from Latin longus. Doublet of allonge.

s.def: A sudden forward movement, especially with a sword.

A long rope or flat web line, more commonly referred to as a lunge line, approximately 20–30 feet long, attached to the bridle, lungeing cavesson, or halter of a horse and used to control the animal while lungeing.
An exercise performed by stepping forward one leg while kneeling with the other leg, then returning to a standing position.
A fish, the namaycush.
To (cause to) make a sudden forward movement (present participle: lunging).
ex: I lunged at the police officer and made a grab for her gun.
With savage desperation the Indian lunged his horse straight at Hopalong and, knife in hand, leaped for him!

s.def: To longe or work a horse in a circle around a handler (present participle: lunging or lungeing).
A rope-like piece of equipment, usually 20 feet or longer in length, attached to the bridle, lungeing cavesson, or halter of a horse to provide control while lungeing.

ety: From lung + fish.

s.def: An air-breathing fish, of the class Dipnoi, that have four limblike appendages instead of fins

ety: From lung + wort. * Having an appearance reminiscent of lungs * Having been used as a treatment for respiratory ailments

s.def: Any of various European plants, of the genus Pulmonaria (family Boraginaceae), that were once used to treat respiratory disorders.
Any of several other, not closely related plants, used to treat respiratory disorders of species:

ety: From luni- + solar.

s.def: Of a calendar, based on both the lunar month and the solar year.
ex: The holidays are all happening within two days this year because several long solar, lunar and lunisolar calendar cycles sync up.

s.def: Pertaining to or caused by both the moon and the sun.

ety: From Middle English lupyne, lupine, from Old French lupin, from Latin lupīnus (“pertaining to the wolf”), because of the wolf-like “fang” within the blossom. It has also been linked to an assumed depletion of nutrients in the soil.

s.def: Any member of the genus Lupinus in the family Fabaceae.

A lupin bean, a yellow legume seed of a Lupinus plant (usually Lupinus luteus), used as feed for sheep and cattle and commonly eaten in the Mediterranean area and in Latin America although toxic if prepared improperly.

ety: Borrowed from Latin lupīnus, from lupus (“wolf”) + -īnus (“pertaining to”). Doublet of lupin and piecewise doublet of wolven, Latin lupus being a cognate of wolf and -ine being a doublet of -en.

s.def: Wolfish (all senses); wolflike.
Ravenous.
North American English form of lupin (any plant of the genus Lupinus; an edible legume seed of one of these plants).

ety: Borrowed from Latin lupus (“wolf”). Doublet of lobo and wolf.

s.def: Any of a number of autoimmune diseases, the most common of which is systemic lupus erythematosus.
ex: You like the name quesalupa? That is a little like "case of lupus". I just keep thinking about that.

ety: From Arabic لُقْمَان (luqmān).

s.def: A sage.
The thirty-first sura (chapter) of the Qur'an, named after the sage.

ety: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of unknown origin. Possibly the same as lurch (“to move stealthily, evade by stooping”) (see below), or from French lâcher (“to let go”).

s.def: To make such a sudden, unsteady movement.
ex: Number One lurched forward, his arms outstretched toward the horror stricken girl.
He was looking for trouble. He lurched against a table at which three soldiers were sitting and knocked over a glass of beer.

s.def: A sudden or unsteady movement.
ex: the lurch of a ship, or of a drunkard

s.def: To swallow or eat greedily; to devour; hence, to swallow up.
ex: Too far off from great cities, which may hinder business; too near them, which lurcheth all provisions, and maketh everything dear.

s.def: To evade by stooping; to lurk; lie in wait; go about in a sneaking way.
To take by surprise; to unexpectedly detain.
To rob.
ex: And in the brunt of seventeen battles since / He lurched all swords of the garland.

s.def: A lift or heave.
A predicament or difficult situation.
ex: to leave someone in the lurch

s.def: An old game played with dice and counters; a variety of the game of tables.
A double score in cribbage for the winner when their adversary has not yet pegged their 31st hole.
ex: August 14, 1784, Horace Walpole, letter to the Hon. H. S. Conway Lady Blandford has cried her eyes out on losing a lurch.

ety: From lurch + -er. See lurch (“to lurk, lie in wait”).

s.def: One who lurks or lies in wait; one who watches in order to rob or betray; a poacher.
A type of crossbreed dog ― a cross between a sighthound and any other breed or the offspring of such crosses.
ex: “Since we are both obsessed with our dogs” — Ms. Muir has a whippet; Ms. Osborne, a lurcher — “we thought we’d try pets,” she said.

s.def: A large nymphalid butterfly, Yoma sabina, of Australia and Asia.
A glutton; a voracious eater
ex: Is not loue a lurcher, that taketh mens stomacks away that they cannot eate, their Spleen that they cannot laugh

ety: From Anglo-Norman lure, from Old French loirre (Modern French leurre), from Frankish *lōþr, from Proto-Germanic *lōþr-, perhaps ultimately related to *laþō (“invitation, calling”), or from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to hide”). Compare English allure, also from Old French. Probably related to German Luder (“bait”).

s.def: An artificial bait attached to a fishing line to attract fish.
ex: the inch-at-a-time flutter of a surface lure

s.def: Something that tempts or attracts, especially one with a promise of reward or pleasure.
ex: How many have with a smile made small account Of Beauty and her lures

s.def: A bunch of feathers attached to a line, used in falconry to recall the hawk.
A velvet smoothing brush.
To attract by temptation, appeal, or guile.
To attract fish with a lure.
To recall a hawk with a lure.
Alternative form of lur.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *loiros Latin lūror Latin lūridusbor. English lurid Borrowed from Latin lūridus (“pale yellow, wan”).

s.def: Pruriently detailed and sensationalistic about something shocking or horrifying, especially with regard to violence or sex.
ex: The accident was described with lurid detail.

s.def: Melodramatic.
Ghastly, pale, wan in appearance.
ex: Fierce o'er their beauty blazed the lurid flame;
Wrapt in drifts of lurid smoke / On the misty river-tide.

s.def: Being of a light yellow hue.
ex: The lurid lighting of the bar made for a very hazy atmosphere.

s.def: Having a brown colour tinged with red.
ex: a lurid plant with maroon leaves and pink flowers

ety: From Middle English lurken, from Old Norse *lúrka, possibly from Proto-Germanic *lūrukōną (“to be lying in wait, lurk”), equivalent to lour + -k (frequentative suffix). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk lurka (“to sneak away, go slowly”), dialectal Swedish lurka (“to dawdle, be slow in one's work”), Saterland Frisian lüürkje (“to look secretly, spy”), West Frisian luorkje (“to lurk”), Middle Low German lûrken (“to deceitfully stalk”).

s.def: To remain concealed in order to ambush.
ex: Things lurking in the dark / They like to leave a mark / Inside of you

s.def: To remain unobserved.
To hang out or wait around a location, preferably without drawing attention to oneself.
ex: if we find the sophist lurking, we must round him up by royal command of the argument

s.def: To read an Internet forum without posting comments or making one's presence apparent.
To saddle (a person) with an undesirable task or duty.
ex: As junior dogsbody, he was lurked with this mission.

s.def: The act of lurking.
ex: At two p.m. a man had called on him, and had produced one of his advertisements, and had asked him if that was all square—no bobbies on the lurk.
There were enemies on the lurk and time was against him.
[…] barked furiously and made at him as at a wolf, and before he could wholly rise from the lurk because of the sudden consternation, […]

s.def: A swindle.

ety: From Arabic لُوسَيْل (lūsayl).

s.def: A city in Al Daayen, Qatar.

ety: From earlier lushious, lussyouse (“luscious, richly sweet, delicious”), a corruption of lustious, from lusty (“pleasant, delicious”) + -ous. Shakespeare uses both lush (short for lushious) and lusty in the same sense: "How lush and lusty the grass looks" (The Tempest ii. I.52). An alternative etymology connects luscious to a Middle English term: lucius, an alteration of licious, believed to be a shortening of delicious.

s.def: Sweet and pleasant; delicious; juicy, succulent.
ex: Her lips were like two luscious beefsteaks.
There were lovely patches of greensward all about, with stately trees bearing rich and luscious fruits.

s.def: Sexually appealing; seductive.
ex: With one hand he gently disclosed the lips of that luscious mouth of nature.

s.def: Obscene.

ety: From Middle English lusch (“slack, relaxed, limp, loose”), from Old English *lysċ, lesċ (“slack; limp”), from Proto-West Germanic *laskwī̆, from Proto-Germanic *laskuz, *laskwaz (“weak, false, feeble”), from Proto-Indo-European *lēy- (“to let; leave behind”). Akin to Old English lysu, lesu (“false, evil, base”), Middle Low German lasch (“slack”), Middle High German er-leswen (“to become weak”), Old Norse lǫskr (“weak, feeble”), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐍃𐌹𐍅𐍃 (lasiws, “weak, feeble”), Middle Low German las…

s.def: Beautiful, sexy.
ex: Boys with long hair are lush!

s.def: Juicy, succulent.
Mellow; soft; (of ground or soil) easily turned; fertile.
Dense, teeming with life; luxuriant.
Savoury, delicious.
ex: That meal was lush! We have to go to that restaurant again sometime!

s.def: Thriving; rife; sumptuous.
Amazing, cool, fantastic, wicked.
ex: Your voice is lush, Lucy! I could listen to it all day!

s.def: Lax; slack; limp; flexible.
A drunkard, sot, alcoholic.
ex: Overaged and lecherous lushes at office parties profaning the text, music, and meaning of Christmas carols.

s.def: Intoxicating liquor.
ex: If your care comes, in the liquor sink it, / Pass along the lush — I'm the boy can drink it.

ety: From Middle English lust, from Old English lust (“lust, pleasure, longing”), from Proto-West Germanic *lustu, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz. Akin to Old Saxon, Dutch lust, Old Frisian, Old High German, German Lust, Swedish lust, Danish lyst, Icelandic lyst, Old Norse losti, Gothic 𐌻𐌿𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (lustus), and perhaps to Sanskrit लष् (laṣ), लषति (laṣati, “to desire”) and Albanian lushë (“bitch, savage dog, promiscuous woman”), or to English loose. Compare list (“to please”), listless.

s.def: A feeling of strong desire, especially such a feeling driven by sexual arousal.
ex: Seeing Leslie fills me with a passionate lust.

s.def: A general want or longing, not necessarily sexual.
ex: The boarders hide their lust to go home.

s.def: A delightful cause of joy, pleasure.
ex: An ideal son is his father's lasting lust.
Pompe, pryde, honour, ryches, and wordly lust, / Parrot sayth playnly, shall tourne all to dust.

s.def: Virility; vigour; active power.
To look at or watch with a strong desire, especially of a sexual nature.
To desire.
Murder for sexual gratification, often involving mutilation.

ety: From Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro, from Old Italian lustrare (“brighten”), from Latin lūstrō (“to purify, to brighten”), from Latin lūstrum (“purification ritual”).

s.def: Shining beauty, splendor, attractiveness or attraction.
ex: After so many years in the same field, the job had lost its luster.
When Autumn's yellow lustre gilds the world...

s.def: Polish, social refinement.
ex: Sure, the posh git spoke with fine lustre. ’S all a load of bollocks, though, innit?

s.def: The ability or condition of shining with reflected light; sheen, gleam, gloss, sparkle, shine, etc.
ex: metallic luster
pearly luster
the diamond’s luster

s.def: Shining light from within, luminosity, brightness, shine.
ex: the sun’s luster
the luster of the minor stars

s.def: Shining fame, renown, glory.
ex: After the scandal, the idol lost his luster and could only get work in Vegas.
Where else then, Denmark? Its misgivings about immigration have smudged some of the liberal lustre it once had.

s.def: A thing exhibiting luster, particularly
ex: The immense room was carpeted, the walls were covered with eighteenth-century panelling, and three electric lustres hung from the ceiling.

s.def: To have luster, to gleam, to shine.
ex: What bloom, what brightness lusters o’er her cheeks!

s.def: To gain luster, to become lustrous.
To give luster, particularly
ex: Our Puritans have from hence learned to colour and lustre their ugly Treasons... with the cloake of Religion.

s.def: To shed light on, to illustrate, to show.

ety: From Middle English lustful, from Old English lustfull (“desirous, wishful”); equivalent to lust + -ful. Cognate with Dutch lustvol (“lustful, lusty”), German lustvoll (“pleasurable”), Swedish lustfyllt (“pleasurable”), Swedish lustfyllda (“lustful”).

s.def: Full of lust; driven by lust.

ety: From Latin lūstrālis, from lūstrum (“purificatory sacrifice”); compare French lustral. See lustrum.

s.def: Of or pertaining to (ritual) purification.
ex: lustral days
lustral water

s.def: Of or relating to a lustrum, or period of five years.
ex: a lustral cycle

ety: From Latin lustrātus (“lustrated”), perfect passive participle of lustrō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lustrum (“ritual purification”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), q.v. In reference to imparting luster, further via senses of Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro.

s.def: Synonym of purify, to ritually cleanse or renew, particularly to do so with a propitiatory offering or (historical) the lustration, quinquennial ritual of the Roman censor to cleanse the city after a census.
ex: We must purge, and cleanse, and lustrate the whole city.
Mid-zenith hangs the fascinated day In wind-lustrated hollows crystalline.

s.def: Synonym of pass through, traverse.
Synonym of look, look over, survey.
Synonym of luster, to impart luster to, to make lustrous.

ety: Etymology tree English lustre Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English lustrous From lustre + -ous.

s.def: Having a glow or lustre.
ex: There was not a cloud on the sky, save a few light vapours that congregated near the moon; but even they were lustrous with her presence.

ety: Borrowed from Latin lūx (“light”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“white; light; bright”).
